title: AI Plan Score
text: The AI Plan Score is a separate AI scoring of your Business Plan. An AI decision model reads what you wrote, step by step, and gives an opinion on how solid the written plan is: how specific, quantified and backed by evidence it is, and whether it settles what a solid 5GDHC business plan has to settle. It is optional and runs only when you start it, on the AI Plan Score page of the dashboard.

title: AI Plan Score · What it is and what it is not
text:
- An AI opinion on the written plan. It rates the text of your Business Plan, not the project itself, and it is marked as AI-generated wherever it appears.
- Not a calculation. The Quick Check stays the only calculation in First Move, with its published equations and default values. The AI Plan Score reads the Quick Check result as context and never changes any of its numbers.
- Not the Pitch completeness. The Pitch completeness counts which fields are filled and does not judge what they say. The AI Plan Score judges the content and leaves the count alone.
- Not a verdict. It is no feasibility study, no jury score and no prediction of funding. Research on venture capital found that business plan documents are only weakly associated with funding decisions (Kirsch, Goldfarb and Gera, 2009). Use the score to find the gaps in your plan.

title: AI Plan Score · What you need
text:
- A Vercel AI Gateway key from your own Vercel account. You bring your own key: the requests run under your account and are billed to it under Vercel's terms.
- Memory only. The key is kept only in the memory of the open tab. It is never written to the browser's storage, to the project or to an export, and it is gone when you reload or close the tab. You can also remove it at any time.
- A Business Plan with content. Empty fields are scored 0 without any AI, so the more you have written, the more the score can say.
- A text model of your choice for the short report and the suggestions: any language model the Gateway offers, picked from a short list or entered by its name.

title: AI Plan Score · What is sent and to whom
AI Plan Score · What is sent and to whom
text:
The Gateway passes the decision questions to TypeSafe AI, which runs the decision model Jev, and the report and the suggestions to the provider of the text model you picked. For the decision model and the listed text models, the app asks the Gateway to use only providers with zero data retention and no training on prompts; for a model you enter by name, it asks for no training on prompts. Vercel offers zero data retention only on its Pro and Enterprise plans, and no training on prompts on every plan. Requests sent with a provider key you added to Vercel yourself (BYOK) fall under your own agreement with that provider. Nothing passes through First Move's servers, and we receive neither your key nor your plan.
Do not put personal data of other people into the plan, such as the names of residents, unless you are allowed to send it. The Privacy Policy and the AI transparency page are the legal reference.

title: AI Plan Score · How it scores
text:
1. Turn 0, without AI. First Move checks which parts of the plan are filled. Empty parts score 0 with certainty and are never sent. When the Quick Check is on and complete, its result enters as context.
2. One decision call per Business Plan step, from the first field to the last: opportunity, business logic, reality check and implementation. In each call the decision model reads the whole plan, so it can check across steps, together with the decisions taken in the earlier steps.
3. Three kinds of questions in each call. A score question for each filled part of that step, on the five evidence levels; gates, which ask yes or no, or pick an option, about the whole plan; and branches, choice questions whose answer selects a follow-up gate for the next step.
4. Aggregation, without AI. The answers become the score, as described under From answers to the score.

title: AI Plan Score · How it scores
text:
The plan has 27 parts in the four steps: 8, 8, 5 and 6. A part is one field, or several fields merged so that the same content is not scored twice, for example the customer segments of the opportunity and of the canvas. The questions are fixed and written in English; your plan may be in English or German. The decision model is pinned to one release, and the method has its own version, so a new model release cannot change a score silently.
If the model declines a question, the call is repeated once without it. A declined part is left out of the score, and a declined gate has no effect.

title: AI Plan Score · The five evidence levels
text:
Every part is rated on the same scale. The levels describe quality, never length: a longer text does not score higher by itself (Brookhart, 2018; Zheng et al., 2023).
- Missing (0): empty, a placeholder, or not about this part or this site.
- Vague (1): a general claim that could fit any project, such as "customers save money", with no named actor, place or number.
- Specific (2): names the actors, buildings, sources or mechanisms of this site, but gives no numbers or no basis for them.
- Quantified (3): the key quantities with units and a stated basis or assumption. A figure quoted from the Quick Check counts as a basis here, not as evidence.
- Evidenced (4): the numbers are backed by named data or commitments, such as metered consumption, a letter of intent, an early check with an authority, a quote or a survey, or they are tested, for example with a break-even value, and the text says what happens if a number is wrong. Claiming that something is validated is not enough.
Each part also has its own description of a strong answer. For the connection rate, for example: a rate with its basis and timeline, the lowest rate at which the plan still works, and what happens below it.

title: AI Plan Score · Gates and caps
text: Gates are questions about the whole plan, and they never add points. A gate passes when the model gives it a probability of 80 % or more, and fails when the probability is 20 % or less; in between it stays unclear and is only flagged. For a gate with options, a partial answer counts half. A failed must-have gate caps its dimension at level 2, a failed should-have gate at level 3, and some gates only flag. A few gates are decided by a rule before any AI: no risk marked as the deal-breaker, an empty connection rate or an empty decision gate fails its gate, and the Vienna heating plan is asked about only when the site is in Vienna.

title: AI Plan Score · Gates and caps
text:
- Anchor customer (Participation and commitment, must-have): does the plan name a specific anchor customer and its role?
- Extra value (Customer value and demand, flag only): does the plan use cooling or another extra value, such as stable prices, as a reason to connect, where it applies?
- Network length as a cost driver (Technical and site fit, must-have when the Quick Check heat density is below 0.5 MWh/m, otherwise flag only): does the plan address the trench length or the heat line density, for example by connecting close buildings first?
- Zone in the Vienna Heating Plan 2040 (Technical and site fit, flag only, in Vienna only): does the plan state the site's zone and why a 5GDHC network fits it?
- System boundary (Ownership, operation and governance, must-have): does the plan say who owns the heat source, the network and the heat pumps in the buildings?
- Operator and duties (Ownership, operation and governance, should-have): does the plan name an operator and its duties, such as maintenance, billing and faults?
- Cost key (Ownership, operation and governance, should-have): does the plan state a rule for splitting the costs of the source, the pipes and the connections?
-

text:
Price against the alternative (Customer value and demand, must-have): is the customer's price compared with the realistic alternative, such as gas or an individual heat pump?
- Minimum connection rate (Participation and commitment, must-have): does the plan say what happens to the costs or the viability if fewer buildings connect?
- Revenues cover the lifetime costs (Costs, revenues and financing, must-have): are the yearly revenues compared with the yearly cost of the investment and the running costs over 20 to 30 years?
- Subsidy fallback (Costs, revenues and financing, must-have): if the plan counts on a subsidy, does it say what happens with less or none?
- Deal-breaker with a validation (Risks, assumptions and evidence, must-have): is one risk marked as the potential deal-breaker, could it really stop the project, and how will it be validated?
- Start small (Implementation path and scalability, should-have): is a first phase defined, such as an anchor cluster, with steps to grow?
- Decision gate (Implementation path and scalability, must-have): do the next steps contain a go or no-go decision with checkable criteria?

title: AI Plan Score · Branches and follow-up gates
text: Branches steer the questions. The model picks the option the plan describes, and the next step asks the follow-up gate of that option only, so a plan built around a school gets other questions than a plan built around a hotel. Most follow-up gates only flag.

title: AI Plan Score · Branches and follow-up gates
text:
- Anchor type (asked in step 1, follow-up in step 2): a public building, a commercial customer, a large residential owner, a waste heat or cooling user, or no anchor. The follow-ups ask about the public decision path, the contract term of a commercial anchor, how owners and tenants decide, or how secure the waste heat or the cooling demand is.
- Main heat source (asked in step 1, follow-up in step 2): groundwater, a borehole field, surface water, wastewater, waste heat, ambient air, or unclear. For groundwater, a borehole field or surface water, the follow-up asks for the permit route or an early check with the water authority. It is a must-have gate for technical and site fit, because the permit is a typical deal-breaker (Wasserrechtsgesetz 1959, § 10). The other sources ask about the sewer operator, the supply agreement for the waste heat, or air in cold weather.
- Ownership model (asked in step 2, follow-up in step 3): a utility, the municipality, the users together, a contractor, a developer, or unclear. The follow-ups ask about the utility's commitment, the municipal decision path, the rules of the community, the contract term and prices, or the operation after handover.

title: AI Plan Score · The seven dimensions
text: The dimensions describe what makes a 5GDHC business plan solid. They start from the aspects for successful implementation named in the study of the research project Anergie Leicht Gemacht: technology, costs, implementation models (ownership and operation, organisation and governance, financing) and participation. The reality check and the path to implementation come from the challenge brief. They were cross-checked against desirability, feasibility and viability (Brown, 2008), the Business Model Canvas (Osterwalder and Pigneur, 2010), the Commercial Readiness Index (ARENA, 2014) and the five-case model of the UK government (HM Treasury, 2026).

title: AI Plan Score · The seven dimensions
text:
- Customer value and demand: 15 %. Who connects, what they need and why the network beats their alternative.
- Technical and site fit: 10 %. The site, its heat sources and resources, and whether the network fits the place.
- Costs, revenues and financing: 20 %. Costs, tariffs, financing and subsidies, and whether revenues cover the costs over the lifetime.
- Ownership, operation and governance: 20 %. Who owns, operates and pays for what, and how costs, risks and benefits are split.
- Participation and commitment: 15 %. Owners, stakeholders, the anchor customer and the connection rate the plan relies on.
- Risks, assumptions and evidence: 10 %. Critical assumptions and risks, the deal-breaker and how each is validated.
- Implementation path and scalability: 10 %. The first phase, the next steps, the decision gate and how the model grows.

title: AI Plan Score · The seven dimensions
text: No source prescribes numeric weights, so these are reasoned defaults. Costs and governance weigh most: the research project calls the implementation models the focus of its work and finds most challenges organisational rather than technical, and costs come first, with the investment upfront and the revenues over 25 to 30 years. Technical fit weighs less, because the Quick Check already screens the site. Evidence weighs less as a dimension, because every part already rewards evidence on its own scale.

title: AI Plan Score · From answers to the score
text:
- A part's level is the probability-weighted mean of the five levels, the expected level, as in G-Eval (Liu et al., 2023). Its spread is the standard deviation of the model's probabilities. An empty part counts 0 with no spread.
- A dimension is the mean of its parts, cut by the lowest cap of its failed gates, times 25, so it runs from 0 to 100.
- The AI Plan Score is the weighted sum of the seven dimensions, from 0 to 100. Its band is one standard deviation, computed from the spreads with the parts taken as independent, which probably makes it too narrow.
- The display rounds the score to 5 points and the band to whole points, at least 1, to avoid false precision.
The score as shown then gets one of three labels:
- Early: below 40.
- Promising: from 40 to below 70, and also 70 or more when a must-have gate failed.
- Solid: 70 or more, with no failed must-have gate.
The label follows the rounded score, so the number you see and its label never contradict each other: a plan at 68 shows 70 and is Solid, unless a must-have gate failed.

title: AI Plan Score · Report and suggestions
text:
- The short report is written by the text model you picked, right after the score: a headline, a summary, up to three strengths and up to three gaps, each pointing to the parts it rests on, and up to three next actions. The model sees the final numbers and short excerpts of the plan.
- Suggestions run on demand, only when you ask: for each part below level 2 and each failed or unclear gate, one to three general and feasible improvements. They are adapted from the description of a strong answer and from sourced hints, such as naming one anchor customer and aiming for a letter of intent.
- The text model never changes a number. The scores are final before it starts. It is told not to recompute or contradict them and not to invent figures, programmes, laws, organisations or sources. Its output is checked and cut to fixed lengths, and pointers to parts that do not exist are dropped.
- Both are marked as AI-generated, like the score.

title: AI Plan Score · Saved in your project
text:
- The last score, with its report and suggestions, is saved in the project in your browser. It is exported and imported with the project file, like your inputs. Your key is never saved.
- Each part keeps a short fingerprint of the text it scored. Once a scored field changes, the score is marked as outdated and says how many parts changed; run it again for a current score. A new run replaces the saved one.
- The score appears on the AI Plan Score page, in the header of every Business Plan step, at the top of the Pitch completeness, on the overview and in the report, always marked as AI-generated.

title: AI Plan Score · Limits and caveats
text:
- AI can be wrong. A model can misread a text or rate it too high or too low. Read the reasons on the AI Plan Score page and check them against your plan.
- The probabilities are not a forecast. They say how sure the model is about which level fits the text, not how likely the project is to succeed, and they are not calibrated.
- Known biases. Models used as judges can prefer longer texts and texts written by AI (Zheng et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023). The levels are written against this, but it cannot be ruled out.
- Structural analogues only. Some sources are UK guidance, such as the HM Treasury business case guidance and the Green Heat Network Fund. They shaped the structure of the gates and are not Austrian or German requirements.
- No advice. The score is not legal, engineering or financial advice, and it never states subsidy rates, eligibility or the outcome of a permit.
- Long plans. Very long texts are shortened before they are sent, so details at the end of a very long text may not be read.

title: AI assistant
text:
The AI assistant is an optional helper in the dashboard. It answers questions about your open project, and it reads documents, such as a PDF or a spreadsheet, into proposed values that you review before they are applied. It works with your own key for an AI provider you choose: your browser talks directly to that provider, and nothing passes through our servers.
The assistant never computes the Quick Check results. The calculation engine does that, with the same equations whether a value was typed in or proposed by the AI.

title: AI assistant · Open the assistant
text: The bot button at the bottom right of every dashboard page opens the assistant as a compact chat. You can expand it into a panel docked on the right side, and the page makes room for it, so the panel covers nothing. On a phone it opens as a full-height sheet. Escape closes it. The assistant is labelled as an AI assistant.

title: AI assistant · Choose a provider and a key
text:
The assistant works with two providers:
- OpenRouter: paste an API key, or choose Connect OpenRouter to sign in there and create a key for First Move without copying it. OpenRouter also offers the Auto Router, which picks a model for each question.
- Vercel AI Gateway: create an API key in your Vercel account and paste it. The same key also runs the AI Plan Score.
The assistant tests the key with the provider before you use it. Requests are billed to your account with the provider, at its prices; First Move itself charges nothing.

title: AI assistant · Pick a model
text: Chips show the price level of each model, from $ to $$$$, and its kind: Fast, Balanced, Best, Frontier or Auto. A tooltip gives the prices, with the date they were checked. The defaults are the Auto Router for OpenRouter and Claude Sonnet 5.5 on the Vercel AI Gateway. You can also enter the id of another model; it must support tool use.

title: AI assistant · Set a spending limit at your provider
text: The assistant is built to keep your key safe, but the real safety net is a spending limit at your provider. Set a spending limit for the key in your provider account before you use it. The assistant asks you to confirm that you have, and you cannot start without confirming. For an OpenRouter key, it shows the limit set on the key, or warns you when there is none.

title: AI assistant · Keep the key for this session or with a PIN
text:
- For this session, the default: the key is kept only in the memory of the browser tab and is gone when you close it.
- Remember on this device: the key is stored encrypted in this browser and locked with a 6-digit PIN, which you enter twice; very common PINs are not accepted. When you come back, you unlock it with the PIN. After five wrong PINs the key is deleted, and you are told why. The key locks again after 30 minutes without use.
The PIN guards against other people who use the same browser. It cannot stop an attack on a copy of your browser profile, so the spending limit at your provider stays the real safety net. The key never goes into project exports, earlier versions or the address bar.

title: AI assistant · What the assistant can see
text:
When you ask a question, the assistant reads the open project: its inputs and its results, and the documents you attach. It sees nothing from your other projects, and it cannot browse the web. To answer, it uses the results of the Quick Check engine, the "How we calculate" explanations with their equation numbers, and these docs pages. Its answers are short and in the language of the app.
Your browser sends each request to the provider you chose, and the provider's terms apply to it. Before you ask, consider what your question and your documents contain: do not send personal data of other people or confidential documents unless you are allowed to. The AI transparency page and the Privacy Policy explain how the AI features handle data.

title: AI assistant · Attach documents
AI assistant · Review proposed values
text:
The assistant never changes your project on its own. Values it reads from a document or a message appear as proposals in a review card. Each row shows the field and its step, the current value, the proposed value with its unit, the quote and page it comes from, and whether it passes the checks. Select the values you want, all or none, and choose Apply selected. Only the selected values are applied, and they go through the same checks as values you type in. When two documents give different values for one field, both are shown, and you decide.
Before you apply a value, check it against the document: that the value really appears there, the unit, the number format (German documents write 1.000,5 where English ones write 1,000.5), the building, area and year it refers to, and whether it is plausible.

title: AI assistant · The AI marks
text: Everything the assistant writes is marked as AI-generated, in the chat and in a machine-readable form. A field value applied from a proposal shows an AI chip, with a tooltip that names the file it came from. The mark is saved in the project and in its export. When you edit the value yourself, it becomes yours, and the chip disappears.

title: AI assistant · Chat history
text: The chat history is kept in this browser, separately for each project, and it is on by default. It holds the messages and the names of attached files, never the text of the documents and never your key, and it keeps at most 200 messages. You can switch it off and clear it in the settings of the assistant. When a project no longer exists, its chat history is deleted the next time you open the assistant.

title: AI assistant · Settings
text: In the settings of the assistant you can change the provider and the model, change your PIN, remove the key, switch the chat history on or off and clear it, and choose how the panel opens. The settings are kept in this browser, but never the key.

title: AI assistant · Remove your key
text: Choose Remove key in the settings of the assistant, and the key is deleted from this browser at once. This does not revoke the key at the provider. To revoke it, delete it in your account there, and do so at once if you think the key was exposed.

title: AI assistant · When something goes wrong
AI assistant · Limits
text: AI models can be wrong. They can misunderstand a question, give a wrong answer with confidence, or invent figures and sources. Reading values from documents is error-prone, especially with scanned pages, tables, units and documents in mixed languages. Check every proposed value, and keep in mind that neither the assistant's answers nor the screening results are engineering advice.

title: Business Plan
text:
The Business Plan is a workspace to develop a business model for a 5GDHC network: who benefits and who pays, who owns and operates the network, what motivates customers to connect, and how investments, revenues and risks are distributed. It follows four suggested steps. You can work on them in any order; the progress is counted per step.
The Business Plan is qualitative. You write in your own words, and it does not calculate anything of its own. When the Quick Check is on, its figures are shown read-only for context. Start in the dashboard with a new project or one of the examples.

title: Business Plan · Step 1: Opportunity
text:
Describe the site or district, the customer segments, the heating and cooling needs, the relevant heat sources and the key pain point. Then explain why a shared low-temperature network offers value compared with the available alternatives, for example individual heat pumps.
You can start from one of the example scenarios or from your own use case. The buildings and the energy sources are shared with the Quick Check: you change them there, and the Business Plan shows them.

title: Business Plan · Step 2: Business logic
text:
Complete a Business Model Canvas for your use case, with particular attention to the value proposition, customer relationships, key partners, operator responsibilities, cost structure and revenue streams. The canvas also holds the key activities, key resources, channels and customer segments.
Then make the allocation of investment, risk and benefit explicit: for each stakeholder, what they invest, which risk they carry and how they benefit.

title: Business Plan · Step 3: Reality check
text: Use rough but transparent assumptions rather than detailed engineering calculations. Test plausible connection rates, tariffs, capital expenditure, financing and subsidy dependencies. Identify the top risks and the top critical assumptions, including one potential deal-breaker, and explain how each could be validated. One risk can be marked as the potential deal-breaker.

title: Business Plan · Step 4: Implementation
text: Refine your business model based on the reality check, expert feedback and the challenges you found. Assess its potential for scalability and replication under different geographical, economic and organisational conditions. Then outline the next practical steps: the data to collect, the stakeholders to engage, the partnerships to secure, the pilot opportunities and the key decisions, including a realistic decision gate for moving the concept forward.

title: Business Plan · Guiding questions
text: Each step shows guiding questions and tips from the challenge brief and from the learnings of the research project Anergie Leicht Gemacht. For example: Who benefits, and who pays? Who owns and who operates the source, the network and the heat pumps? Connecting is voluntary, so what makes owners say yes? Use what helps.

title: Business Plan · Example scenarios
text: Four predefined scenarios can start a Business Plan (BM-SCN-01 to BM-SCN-04). Picking one fills in only what the scenario states. You can change everything afterwards, and the app asks before a scenario replaces text you wrote. You can also describe your own use case instead.

title: Business Plan · Example scenarios
text:
- Scenario 01, rural village: private households and a hotel; private ownership, tourist accommodation and commercial use; other partners: the municipality and a ski resort; 20-70 units in phased development; current energy supply not specified.
- Scenario 02, urban outskirts with no district heating planned: a secondary school, a kindergarten and multi-family buildings; municipal ownership and rental apartments; other partner: the owner of the educational facilities; about 80 units; current energy supply natural gas.
- Scenario 03, urban outskirts with mixed ownership: private homeowners, housing cooperatives, the municipality and educational facilities; condominium ownership (WEG), rental housing (MRG) and non-profit housing (WGG); other partners to be identified; 3-20 buildings; current energy supply natural gas and biomass.
- Scenario 04, urban outskirts with a thermal spa and hotels: a thermal spa, hotels and private households; mainly tourism and spa facilities, limited residential use; other partners to be identified; 3-20 buildings; current energy supply natural gas and biomass.

title: Business Plan · Example scenarios
text: The start screen also offers six illustrative example projects with both modules filled in, four of them based on these scenarios. Opening one creates your own copy.

title: Business Plan · Pitch completeness (unofficial)
text:
The last step shows how complete your pitch is: how much of the final pitch already has content, from what you filled in. It counts filled fields only and does not judge the content, and it is labelled unofficial.
It checks the six parts of the final pitch (BM-SCOPE-07): the use case and value proposition, the business model, the economic and practical feasibility, the reality check, the scalability and replicability, and the next steps. Next to them it shows the jury criteria proposed in the first version of the challenge brief (BM-SCOPE-08). They are not an official scoring rule.
Each part has a short list of points. A text point counts when its field has text, a list point when it has an entry, and a risk or critical-assumption point when at least one row is complete and no row is half filled. The share of points covered is the score of the part, and the completeness is the average of the six parts. A part is complete when all its points are covered. There is no equation behind this, and no judgement of the content.

title: Business Plan · AI Plan Score
text: For a judgement of the content, the optional AI Plan Score gives an AI opinion on how solid the written plan is. It is shown before the Pitch completeness, bolder, in the header of every step and at the top of the completeness panel, and it is marked as AI-generated. It runs only when you start it, with your own Vercel AI Gateway key, and it never changes the Quick Check or the Pitch completeness. The AI Plan Score page explains how it scores, what is sent and the sources behind it.

title: Business Plan · Quick Check figures in the Business Plan
text: When the Quick Check is on and complete, the Business Plan shows its rough figures for context: the heating and cooling demand, the revenue and the overall investment, next to the buildings, the project area and the selected sources. They are screening values, not a feasibility study, and they are read-only: you change the inputs in the Quick Check. With your own parameters, they carry the "Custom parameters" badge. The sources screened in the Quick Check can be added to the heat sources text with one click.

title: Business Plan · Comparing business models
text: A project holds one business model. To compare an alternative, duplicate the project and change the copy.

title: Data and privacy
text: First Move keeps your work on your device. There is no account and no password, and the projects you create are stored only in the browser you use. We never receive them, so we cannot read, share or recover them.

title: Data and privacy · Where your projects live
text:
Your projects, settings and choices are stored only in your browser's storage: the projects in its database (IndexedDB), with a copy of each project in its local storage as a safeguard. They stay in this browser on this device. Another browser or another device does not see them, and a private window may not keep them at all.
First Move asks your browser to keep this storage persistent, so that the browser is less likely to remove your projects on its own. Your browser decides whether to grant this.

title: Data and privacy · Saving
text: First Move saves every change automatically, and the save status in the top bar shows when the project was last saved; there is no save button. If the same project is open in two tabs, they stay in sync. If both tabs change it, your version is kept, and the other one is saved as an earlier version.

title: Data and privacy · Export and import
text:
- Export saves the open project as a .firstmove.json file, wherever you choose. The file holds your inputs and, if you ran one, the last AI Plan Score. The calculated results are not stored; they are calculated again when the file is imported.
- Import reads a .firstmove.json file and checks it in your browser; nothing is uploaded. If the project is already in this browser, you choose whether to keep both or to replace the stored version. A replaced version is kept, so you can restore it.
- A file from an earlier version of First Move is updated to the current format when you import it.
- Report shows the open project as a printable page. Your browser prints it or saves it as a PDF; nothing is uploaded.
Export your projects regularly, because an export is your copy outside this browser. First Move reminds you to export from time to time.

title: Data and privacy · Earlier versions
text:
While you work, First Move keeps earlier versions of each project in this browser, up to 20 per project, for example before a restore, an import or a delete. Restore a version in the project menu brings one back, and the current state is kept as a version too.
In Chromium-based browsers, Link to a file in the project menu also saves the project to a file on your own disk. The file stays on your disk, and nothing is uploaded.

title: Data and privacy · Deleting data
text:
- Delete a project from the project menu or from the list on the start screen. You can undo this only right after deleting, while the message is shown, so export the project first if you want to keep a copy.
- Clear the site data of First Move in your browser's settings to delete everything it stored there: all projects, earlier versions and settings. We cannot recover them, because we never had them.

title: Data and privacy · Cookies and settings
text: First Move sets one functional cookie, which remembers your language. Your theme and your other settings are kept in your browser's storage. The website has no tracking, no advertising and no third-party cookies, so there is nothing to accept. The Cookie Policy lists every cookie and storage entry by name.

title: Data and privacy · The AI Plan Score and your data
text:
The optional AI Plan Score runs only when you start it, with your own Vercel AI Gateway key. Your browser then sends the open project's Business Plan texts and, when available, the Quick Check result directly to the Vercel AI Gateway, under your own account. Nothing goes through our servers, and we receive neither the content nor the key.
- The key stays in memory. It is kept only in the memory of the open tab, never in the browser's storage, the project or an export, and it is gone when you reload or close the tab.
- The score is saved in the project. The last score, with its report and suggestions, is stored with the project in your browser and is part of an export, marked as AI-generated. A new run replaces it.
The Privacy Policy names the recipients and the AI transparency page explains how the score is classified.

title: Data and privacy · The AI features and your data
text:
Besides the AI Plan Score, First Move has two optional AI layers, separate from the app and from each other. The AI transparency page says whether they are available today.
- The AI assistant in the dashboard works with your own key for an AI provider you choose. When you use it, your browser sends your request directly to that provider: your question, the open project's inputs and results, and the documents you attach; nothing from your other projects. We receive neither the content nor the key. The key stays in your browser, for the session only or locked with a PIN on this device, and the chat history stays in your browser too.
- The email agent at agent@mail.firstmove.energy processes what you send to it on the server, through the service providers named in the Privacy Policy, and only after you have confirmed once. The conversation is stored encrypted, for 30 days after your last message.
The Quick Check results and the Pitch completeness never come from AI, and the projects in your browser never go to our servers.
The AI assistant and Email agent pages explain both in detail.

title: Data and privacy · Legal pages
text: The legal pages are the reference: the Privacy Policy, the Cookie Policy, the Terms of Use, the AI transparency page and the Imprint. For privacy questions and requests about your rights, write to human@mail.firstmove.energy, which is read by a person.

title: Email agent
text:
You can also use First Move by email: write to agent@mail.firstmove.energy. This mailbox is answered by an AI system. It answers short questions about First Move and fifth-generation district heating and cooling from these public docs, and it can run a Quick Check, a Business Plan or both with you by email. For now, the email agent writes in English.
For privacy questions, legal matters and requests about your data protection rights, write to human@mail.firstmove.energy instead. That mailbox is read by a person.

title: Email agent · What it can do
text:
- Answer questions about First Move, 5GDHC, the Quick Check and the Business Plan, using only these docs. When the docs do not cover a question, it says so.
- Run a Quick Check by email: it asks for the inputs and sends you the result.
- Develop a Business Plan by email, step by step.
- Send a project file that you can import in the dashboard, if you want one.
Replies are written by an AI system and sent automatically; a person does not review them. They may be wrong, and they are not legally binding.

title: Email agent · The first email: confirm once
text:
The first time you write, nothing is processed by AI. Your message waits, unread, and you get a short email with a confirmation link. On the confirmation page, tick the box and press the button: you accept the Terms of Use and emails about your request, with no marketing. Then your message is processed.
If you do not confirm within 7 days, your message is never processed. If you did not write to us, ignore the email. You confirm only once; your confirmation is kept for 12 months after your last message.

title: Email agent · Who can write
text: Your mail provider must authenticate your email (DMARC); most providers do. Email that does not pass this check is ignored, without a reply. Automatic replies, mailing lists and bounces are ignored as well. The agent replies only to the address the email came from, and never to anyone else.

title: Email agent · A Quick Check by email
text:
1. First the agent asks which module you want, 1 Quick Check, 2 Business Plan or 3 both, and whether you would like a project file to import in the dashboard, yes or no. A short answer such as "1, yes" or "both, no" works, and so does writing it in your own words.
2. For a Quick Check, it sends a numbered list of questions, each with an example answer: the project name (optional), the number of buildings, the project area in m² (hectares work too), the building mix by type and construction period (it must add up to 100 %), the energy sources and their potential, whether PV is available, and, if you know them, the heating and cooling demand in kWh/a and the network length in m.
3. Answer with the number of the question, for example "2: 40 buildings". You can answer in several emails, and correct a value the same way or in words, for example "change the area to 4 ha".
4. Each reply lists what the agent understood, what is unclear and what is still missing.
5. When the required inputs are complete, you get the result.

title: Email agent · A Quick Check by email
text: The result is calculated by First Move's own Quick Check engine, exactly as in the dashboard; the AI only collects your inputs. The Quick Check page explains how the result is calculated.

title: Email agent · A Business Plan by email
text:
For a Business Plan, the agent goes through the four steps, one round each: the opportunity, the business logic, the reality check and the implementation. Each round brings the guiding questions of the step, with the example scenarios as examples. Your answers are kept in your own words. When you choose both modules, the Business Plan shows the Quick Check figures read-only.
The summary lists the filled sections, the critical assumptions, the risks and the Pitch completeness checklist, which is unofficial. The Business Plan page explains the steps.

title: Email agent · Attaching files to an email
Email agent · Results and the project file
text:
The Quick Check result comes as an email in the style of First Move, with a plain-text version: the overall result and its main factors, the key figures, the assumptions and how the figures were calculated, the inputs used, and the note that this is a screening, not a feasibility study. A Business Plan comes as a summary of the same kind. There is no PDF report yet.
If you asked for a project file, a .firstmove.json file is attached. Import it in the dashboard to continue there; the values collected by email carry an AI mark. You can also ask for the file later by writing "file".
After the result, further answers update it, and the agent sends it again. Write "new" to start over, or "stop" to end the conversation and delete it.

title: Email agent · The rules
text:
The mailbox is for questions about First Move and fifth-generation district heating and cooling, and for your Quick Check and Business Plan. Greetings and thanks are fine.
- Stay on topic. A first off-topic email gets one warning. A second one pauses the mailbox for you for 30 days.
- No misuse. Attempts to manipulate the assistant, to reveal its instructions or to make it email other people, harassment, and fraud, phishing, malware or spam block the sender. You get one notice, and the operator is told what happened.
- After a pause or a block, the agent does not reply.
When the agent is not sure whether an email is misuse, it counts the email as a warning rather than a block.

title: Email agent · How long data is kept
text:
- An unconfirmed first message waits for your confirmation for 7 days.
- The conversation: 30 days after your last message.
- A warning: 90 days. A pause: 30 days. A block: until we delete it.
- Your confirmation: 12 months after your last message.
For these records your address is stored only in hashed form, and the conversation and the list of waiting messages are stored encrypted. The emails themselves stay with our email provider for 30 days. Our emails carry minimal open and click tracking (E-mail tracking). The Privacy Policy has the details.

title: Email agent · Who processes your email
text: To answer, your email and its attachments are processed by these service providers: Resend for email, Vercel for the functions, the workflows and the AI Gateway, TypeSafe AI for Jev, a decision model that checks each email for relevance and misuse, Anthropic for Claude Haiku, which reads the email and writes the answer, and Upstash for the encrypted records. The Privacy Policy names them with their locations and safeguards.

title: Introduction
text: First Move is a free web app for the first steps of a fifth-generation district heating and cooling (5GDHC) project. It helps municipalities, energy service providers and other project initiators to screen a project area and to develop a business model for a network there.

title: Introduction · Two modules
text:
A project in First Move has two optional modules. You can use one of them or both, and you can turn each one on or off at any time; the data of a module is kept while it is off.
- Quick Check: a first assessment of the technical and economic potential of a 5GDHC network for a project area. You enter a few key parameters, and the Quick Check applies a predefined calculation and assessment methodology. The result is one of three levels, Promising, Further analysis required or Not promising, shown together with the main factors behind it.
- Business Plan: a workspace to develop a business model for the network in four steps, from the opportunity to the next steps towards implementation. You write in your own words; the Business Plan calculates nothing of its own.
Both modules share the site data, such as the buildings and the energy sources, so you enter them once.

title: Introduction · Your data stays in your browser
text: There is no account, and your projects are stored only in the browser you use. First Move never receives them. Export a project to keep a copy or to move it to another browser. Data and privacy explains the details.

title: Introduction · Where to start
text:
1. Open the dashboard.
2. Start a new project with the Quick Check, the Business Plan or both, or open one of the six examples. Opening an example creates your own copy; the examples use illustrative inputs only.
3. Or import a project file (.firstmove.json) that you exported before.
New to 5GDHC? Read What is 5GDHC? first.

title: Introduction · Read next
text:
- What is 5GDHC?: the idea behind the networks, where they fit and where they do not.
- Quick Check: every input, how the result is calculated and what it means.
- Business Plan: the four steps, the example scenarios and the Pitch completeness checklist.
- AI Plan Score: the optional AI opinion on how solid your written Business Plan is, with your own key.
- Data and privacy: where your projects live, export, import and deleting data.
- AI assistant: the optional assistant in the dashboard, with your own key.
- Email agent: a Quick Check or a Business Plan by email.

title: Introduction · A screening, not a feasibility study
text: The Quick Check gives an initial indication, not a definitive feasibility decision. Its parameters and methodology are based on simplified assumptions; actual values may vary with project-specific conditions and should be refined through further analysis. Neither the results nor these pages are engineering advice.

title: Quick Check
text:
The Quick Check gives a first assessment of the technical and economic potential of a 5GDHC network for a project area. You enter a few key parameters. The Quick Check estimates the energy demand, the network length, the supply coverage and the economics, classifies the indicators and gives one of three overall results, together with the main factors behind it. It communicates an initial indication, not a definitive feasibility decision.
The calculation follows a predefined 5GDHC Quick Check methodology; First Move implements it and does not change it. On this page, equations are cited by their number in the methodology (for example EQ-3.4a) and default tables by theirs (for example TBL-6). Where the methodology leaves a point open, the answer First Move applies is cited by its number (for example OQ-20). In the app, every input step and every result has a "How we calculate" section with the equations used.

title: Quick Check · The steps
text:
The Quick Check has four input steps and a results page:
1. Project area: the number of buildings and the project area.
2. Buildings: the share of each building type and construction period.
3. Energy sources: the sources available in the area and their potential.
4. Options: a known demand, a known network length and photovoltaics, all optional.
5. Results: the overall result, the main factors, the indicators and the key figures.
The result appears as soon as the required inputs are complete: the number of buildings, the project area, shares that add up to 100 % and at least one energy source. All calculations run automatically, in your browser. The Assumptions page shows every default value and lets you try your own parameters.

title: Quick Check · Number of buildings
text:
The total number of buildings in the project area, as a whole number, including industrial buildings. Together with the project area it gives the building density (EQ-3.3). It also sets the number of buildings in each group (EQ-3.1), the heat pump investment, with one heat pump per building (EQ-3.10d), and the connection fees (EQ-3.9c).
Where to find it: a map of the area, the building or address register of the municipality, or a walk through the area.

title: Quick Check · Project area
text:
The total project area in m². The app shows the value in hectares next to it; 1 ha is 10,000 m². The area sets the building density in buildings per hectare (EQ-3.3) and, unless you enter a network length, the estimated network length (EQ-3.4b).
Where to find it: draw the area on a map or in a GIS tool, or take it from a land-use or development plan.

title: Quick Check · Building types and construction periods
text:
Enter the share of each building type and construction period in %, in a grid with the building types as rows and the construction periods as columns. All shares must add up to 100 %; until they do, there is no result.
- Residential buildings: residential buildings of different construction periods.
- Category A: retail, museums, supermarkets, schools, offices and fitness studios.
- Category B: kindergartens, sports halls, hotels and theatres.
- Category C: hospitals, restaurants, swimming pools and canteens.
- Industry: industrial buildings and facilities.
The construction periods are -1919, 1919-1960, 1961-1990, 1991-2010 and 2011-today, labelled as in the methodology; no calculation depends on the boundary year (OQ-03).
For example, a project area could consist of 50 % residential buildings from 1991-2010, 25 % residential buildings from 2011-today and 25 % Category A buildings from 2011-today.

title: Quick Check · Building types and construction periods
text:
Industry has no default values. An industry share adds no demand, no floor area and no base-price or energy-price revenue, and any industry share sets the overall result to "Further analysis required" (OQ-02). Industrial buildings still count in the number of buildings, for example in the building density, the connection fees and the heat pump investment (OQ-02).
Where to find it: the building register or census statistics of the municipality, energy performance certificates, or a walk through the area.

title: Quick Check · Heating and cooling demand
text:
The shares split the number of buildings into groups: the number of buildings of a type and period is the total number of buildings times its share (EQ-3.1). Shares and other percentages are divided by 100 first, and a group may hold a fractional number of buildings (OQ-01).
Each group gets the default annual heating demand per m² of floor area (TBL-1), the default annual cooling demand per m² (TBL-2) and the default floor area per building (TBL-3) of its type and construction period. The number of buildings times the demand per m² times the floor area gives the annual heating and cooling demand of each group (EQ-3.2a, EQ-3.2b). The sum over all groups is the total annual heating demand and the total annual cooling demand of the project area (EQ-3.2c, EQ-3.2d). A known demand that you enter in Options replaces these totals.

title: Quick Check · Energy sources
text:
Select the energy sources that are available or potentially available in the project area, and rate the potential of each one: Low, Medium, High or Unknown. You can select several sources; their supplies add up (OQ-11).
For each source, the Quick Check takes the predefined annual capacity of its potential, TBL-4 for heating and TBL-5 for cooling, and the COP of its heat pump. The capacities are the energy taken from the source, not the energy delivered to the buildings; the COP of the heat pump turns them into the supply (see Supply).
- Solar thermal has no COP in the methodology, so its capacity counts as heating supply directly, without heat pump electricity (OQ-13).
- Waste heat and solar thermal have no default cooling capacity, so they supply no cooling (OQ-13).
- An Unknown potential adds no supply. It sets the overall result to "Further analysis required", because the potential needs to be clarified before a reliable initial assessment can be made.

title: Quick Check · Energy sources
text:
The methodology does not say whether the capacities apply per project, per building or per area. First Move applies them as absolute values per selected source for the whole project and flags this on the Assumptions page (OQ-26). With the default capacities, the sources cover the demand of small projects only: one residential building needs about 30,000 to 68,000 kWh/a of heat, while the highest default capacity of a source is 150,000 kWh/a. You can try other capacities with Play with parameters.
Where to find it: geological and hydrogeological maps, studies of the area, the operator of a possible waste-heat source, or the authorities responsible for water and geology. If you cannot rate a source yet, choose Unknown.

title: Quick Check · Options
text:
All options are optional. Leave a field empty to keep the estimate of the methodology.
- Known heating and cooling demand: if you have more detailed information about the buildings' energy demand, enter the total annual heating demand and the total annual cooling demand in kWh/a. Each value replaces the estimated total (EQ-3.2c, EQ-3.2d) wherever the total is used; the base-price revenues still use the default floor areas (OQ-05).
- Network length: if you know the estimated total network length, enter it in m. It replaces the estimate (EQ-3.4a, EQ-3.4b), and the results say that the length was entered.
- Photovoltaic (PV) available: with PV, the electricity costs of the heat pumps are lowered by the PV cost reduction of 30 % (TBL-6, OQ-06).
Where to find it: energy bills, meter data or the energy supplier for the demand; a first network sketch for the length.

title: Quick Check · Building density
text:
The building density is the number of buildings per hectare of project area (EQ-3.3). It is classified with TBL-8:
- High density: above 30 buildings/ha. Densely built areas can benefit from shorter network lengths, although low energy demand may still weaken economic performance.
- Medium density: from 10 to 30 buildings/ha. The structure may be suitable for a network.
- Low density: below 10 buildings/ha. Buildings are more distributed, potentially increasing network length. High energy demand or suitable local energy sources may still make a project promising.
The building density category (rural, sub-urban or urban) is not an input. It follows from this class: low density is rural, medium is sub-urban, high is urban (OQ-04).

title: Quick Check · Network length
text:
Unless you enter a network length, the Quick Check estimates it in two steps. First, the specific network length in metres per hectare follows from the building density with a predefined relationship (EQ-3.4a); the number of buildings per hectare in that equation is the building density (OQ-09). Then the specific network length times the project area in hectares gives the total network length in metres (EQ-3.4b).
The results always say whether the network length was entered or estimated.

title: Quick Check · Heat density
text:
The heat density is the total annual heating demand divided by the network length (EQ-3.5). Higher heat density can improve the economic outlook, because more heating demand is served per metre of network. It is calculated in kWh per metre and classified in MWh per metre (OQ-10), with TBL-9:
- High density: above 1.5 MWh/m. A relatively short network serves a high heating demand, potentially improving economic performance.
- Medium density: from 0.5 to 1.5 MWh/m. The network may be viable.
- Low density: below 0.5 MWh/m. A relatively long network serves a low heating demand. Substantial cooling demand or low network costs may improve the outlook.

title: Quick Check · Supply
text: For each selected source, the heating supply is its capacity plus the share the heat pump adds: capacity times COP / (COP − 1) (EQ-3.8a). The cooling supply is its cooling capacity adjusted by the COP: capacity times COP / (COP + 1) (EQ-3.8b). COP is the coefficient of performance of the heat pump; the heating COP comes from TBL-4 and the cooling COP from TBL-5 (OQ-14). The supplies of all selected sources are added up (OQ-11).

title: Quick Check · Coverage
text:
The coverage is the share of the annual demand that the selected sources can supply: the heating supply divided by the heating demand (EQ-3.6a), and the cooling supply divided by the cooling demand (EQ-3.6b). A value of 1.0 corresponds to 100 % coverage. Heating and cooling coverage are shown and classified separately, so supply gaps stay visible (TBL-7):
- Feasible: 100 % or more. Sufficient annual energy potential to cover the total demand with additional potential available.
- Conditionally feasible: from 90 % to below 100 %. A small share of supplementary supply is required.
- Limited feasibility: from 70 % to below 90 %. A significant share of supplementary supply is required.
- Not feasible as the sole supply concept: below 70 %. Too much demand remains uncovered.
A demand of 0 is not relevant, so it gets no coverage class (OQ-22).

title: Quick Check · Cooling-to-heating ratio
text:
The cooling-to-heating ratio indicates how balanced the annual heating and cooling demands are. The methodology gives no formula for it (EQ-3.7). First Move divides the smaller of the two demands by the larger one, so the ratio is always between 0 and 1, and names the demand that is higher (OQ-12). A value of 1 indicates equal demands; values approaching 0 indicate an increasing imbalance. When both demands are 0, the ratio is not applicable. It is classified with TBL-10:
- Balanced: 0.8 or more. Heating and cooling demand are similar, potentially supporting thermal exchange.
- Partially balanced: from 0.3 to below 0.8. One demand is higher than the other, but thermal exchange may still be possible.
- Unbalanced: below 0.3. One demand clearly dominates, potentially increasing the need for external energy sources or thermal storage.
The ratio indicates the potential for thermal balancing. It does not decide on its own whether a network is feasible, but it can influence the system configuration and the economic viability. An unbalanced demand profile does not automatically make a 5GDHC network unsuitable.

title: Quick Check · Revenues
text:
- Heating revenue: the heating base price for every m² of floor area per year, plus the heating energy price for every kWh of heating demand (EQ-3.9a). The base prices are per m² of floor area and year (OQ-16), and the floor area is the default floor area of each building group (TBL-3).
- Cooling revenue: the cooling base price for every m² of floor area per year, plus the cooling energy price for every kWh of cooling demand (EQ-3.9b, OQ-15).
- Overall revenues: the heating revenue, the cooling revenue and the connection fees. The connection fee is a one-time fee per building, spread over the depreciation period with the annuity factor (EQ-3.9c).

title: Quick Check · Costs
text:
- Network investment: the network construction costs per metre times the network length (EQ-3.10a).
- Installation investment: for each selected source, its installation costs per kWh/a times its heating supply (EQ-3.10b), summed over all sources (EQ-3.10c). TBL-6 gives no installation costs for ambient air; First Move uses 0, because the heat pumps are already counted in the heat pump investment (OQ-18).
- Overall investment: the investment in one heat pump times the number of buildings, plus the network investment and the installation investment of all sources (EQ-3.10d). The installations are counted once (OQ-17).
- Annualized costs: the overall investment times the annuity factor (EQ-3.10f). The annuity factor turns an investment into equal yearly payments over the depreciation period at the interest rate (EQ-3.10e).
- Electricity costs: for each source, the heating supply divided by the heating COP and the cooling supply divided by the cooling COP, times the electricity price, in € per year (EQ-3.11, OQ-19). With PV, they are multiplied by 1 − 0.30 (OQ-06).
- Operation and maintenance: 0.02 times the overall investment, that is 2 % of it every year (EQ-3.12).

title: Quick Check · Economic assessment
text:
The methodology does not define when the economic assessment is favorable or clearly unfavorable, so First Move uses an economic ratio E (OQ-21): the overall revenues divided by the annual costs, which are the annualized costs plus the electricity costs plus operation and maintenance.
- Favorable: E is 1.0 or more. The revenues cover the annual costs.
- Unclear: E is 0.7 or more, but below 1.0. The revenues cover a large part, but not all, of the annual costs.
- Clearly unfavorable: E is below 0.7. The revenues fall far short of the annual costs.
The economic parameters (TBL-6) are only preliminary assumptions, so treat the economic results with care.

title: Quick Check · The verdict: what the overall result means
text:
The overall result, the verdict of the Quick Check, is one of three levels:
- Promising: favorable conditions identified.
- Further analysis required: mixed conditions, uncertainties or missing information.
- Not promising: unfavorable conditions identified.
The indicator is intentionally broad, to avoid false precision and to make clear that it is a general initial assessment, not a detailed feasibility study. It combines the supply coverage, the building and heat density and the economic assessment (TBL-11), checked in this order (OQ-22):
1. Set by a fixed rule: if the project area includes industry, or if any selected source has an Unknown potential, the result is "Further analysis required".
2. Not promising: if the economic assessment is clearly unfavorable, or if a relevant supply coverage is below 70 % and both the building density and the heat density are low.
3. Promising: if there is at least one relevant demand, every relevant demand has at least 90 % annual supply coverage, the economic assessment is favorable, and neither the building density nor the heat density is low.
4. Further analysis required: in every other case.
A demand is relevant when it is above 0 (OQ-22).

title: Quick Check · Main factors
text:
Next to the overall result, the Quick Check shows the main factors supporting or limiting it, and under "Why this result" the reasons for the level it reached.
- An indicator supports the result when it meets its condition for Promising: a coverage of at least 90 %, a favorable economic assessment, a building density or heat density that is not low.
- It limits the result otherwise.
- Industry in the project area and an Unknown source potential always limit the result.
- A demand of 0 is left out. The cooling-to-heating ratio is shown with its class but not counted as a factor, because it does not decide the result on its own.

title: Quick Check · Limits of the Quick Check
text:
- A screening, not engineering advice. The Quick Check is intended for a preliminary screening rather than a detailed system design. It does not replace a detailed technical or economic feasibility study.
- Simplified assumptions. The parameters, inputs and methodology are based on simplified assumptions and should be interpreted carefully. Actual values may vary with project-specific conditions and should be refined through further analysis.
- Your inputs only. The Quick Check does not query external databases. It works with what you enter and the default values.
- The same inputs give the same result. The calculation is deterministic and runs in your browser; it does not use AI.
- Illustrative examples. The example projects on the start screen use illustrative inputs only.

text:

title: What is 5GDHC?
text: 5GDHC stands for fifth-generation district heating and cooling. A 5GDHC network is a low-temperature system that supplies buildings with heating and cooling. Such networks are also called anergy networks or ambient loop networks.

title: What is 5GDHC? · A low-temperature network
text:
Water circulates in a 5GDHC network at around 5 to 25 °C. At these temperatures the network can use renewable energy and waste heat efficiently without insulated pipes, and its losses are minimal.
The network connects the buildings with energy sources and with thermal storage, such as borehole fields, buffer tanks or seasonal storage.

title: What is 5GDHC? · Heat pumps in every building
text: Each building uses its own heat pump to provide heating or cooling. The decentralised heat pumps raise the temperature to what each building needs, for radiators or for floor heating. The challenge: a higher upfront investment and more complex control.

title: What is 5GDHC? · Sharing heat and cold
text: A key advantage is the bidirectional energy exchange. Excess heat can be fed back into the network and used by other buildings, which improves the overall energy efficiency. When some buildings heat while others cool, their demands balance each other, so summer cooling becomes a reason to connect.

title: What is 5GDHC? · Typical sources
text:
Typical sources are groundwater, geothermal energy, waste heat and wastewater. The Quick Check works with six kinds of source: geothermal, waste heat, ground water, surface water, solar thermal and ambient air.
In the use cases of the research project Anergie Leicht Gemacht, groundwater was the most economical source.

title: What is 5GDHC? · Why it matters
text: 5GDHC networks integrate renewable energy and waste heat efficiently and reduce the reliance on fossil fuels. They can also contribute to a resilient, secure and locally available energy supply, because they integrate local energy sources, reduce the dependence on individual energy carriers and allow a flexible exchange and storage of heat and cold.

title: What is 5GDHC? · Where it fits
text:
5GDHC networks can be built in different settlement and building types, but they need suitable technical and economic conditions. The research project Anergie Leicht Gemacht drew these learnings from its use cases:
- Existing buildings can be integrated, most of them even without major thermal renovation.
- Heat line density decides the economics: above about 1 MWh per metre of trench, networks can beat individual solutions.
- Pipes and house connections drive the cost; the trench length dominates the investment.
- Micro-networks between direct neighbours are a promising option.
Good to know: the investment comes first, while the revenues come over 25 to 30 years, and every building that stays out raises the costs for the rest.

title: What is 5GDHC? · Where it is harder
text:
The Quick Check indicators show what can weaken the case for a network:
- Low building density: the buildings are more spread out, which can increase the network length.
- Low heat density: a relatively long network serves a low heating demand.
- Unbalanced demand: when heating or cooling clearly dominates, more external energy sources or thermal storage may be needed. An unbalanced demand profile does not automatically make a 5GDHC network unsuitable.
Most challenges are organisational rather than technical: coordination, ownership structures, financing and long-term operation. In the experience of the project, connecting is voluntary, and many owners decide individually: homeowners, housing associations and public buildings.

title: What is 5GDHC? · Examples in practice
text:
- Viertel Zwei, Vienna: residential, commercial and public buildings with decentralised heat pumps, on geothermal energy, wastewater and groundwater; in operation since 2017.
- Bregenz, Vorarlberg: water from Lake Constance as the source for heating and cooling, run by the municipal utility, Stadtwerke Bregenz; in operation, and the network is being expanded.
- Lagarde, Bamberg: existing and new buildings with about 1,200 dwellings, 70 decentralised heat pumps and 5.5 km of pipe, on geothermal energy and wastewater heat; in operation since 2023, with Stadtwerke Bamberg.

title: What is 5GDHC? · How First Move helps
text: The Quick Check screens a project area: does a 5GDHC network look promising there, and which factors decide it? The Business Plan helps you work out who benefits and who pays, who owns and operates the network, and which risks could stop it.

title: How we calculate · Quick Check · Project area
text: The number of buildings and the project area give the building density in buildings per hectare. Unless you enter a network length, the tool estimates the length from this density. The number of buildings also sets the heat pump investment and the connection fees.

title: How we calculate · Quick Check · Buildings
text: The shares split the buildings into types and construction periods. Each group gets the default heating demand, cooling demand and floor area of Tables 1 to 3; together they give the total annual demand. Industry has no default values: it adds no demand and leads to “Further analysis required”.

title: How we calculate · Quick Check · Energy sources
text: Each selected source adds the default annual capacity of its potential (Tables 4 and 5). The heat pump turns it into delivered heating and cooling, which sets the coverage, the installation costs and the electricity costs. A source with unknown potential adds nothing and leads to “Further analysis required”.

title: How we calculate · Quick Check · Options
text: A known heating or cooling demand replaces the estimated total, and a known network length replaces the estimated length. PV lowers the electricity costs of the heat pumps by the PV cost reduction of Table 6.

title: How we calculate · Quick Check · Assumptions
text: A changed parameter replaces the default of Tables 4 to 6 in every equation that uses it. Results then carry the “Custom parameters” badge.

title: How we calculate · Heating demand
text:
The buildings of each type and construction period times their default heating demand per m² and their default floor area, summed over all groups.
You entered the total heating demand, so it replaces the estimate.

title: How we calculate · Cooling demand
text:
The buildings of each type and construction period times their default cooling demand per m² and their default floor area, summed over all groups.
You entered the total cooling demand, so it replaces the estimate.

title: How we calculate · Building density
text: The number of buildings per hectare of project area.

title: How we calculate · Building density category
text: Follows from the building density class of Table 8: low density is rural, medium is sub-urban, high is urban.

title: How we calculate · Specific network length
text: Network metres per hectare, estimated from the building density with the predefined relationship of the methodology.

title: How we calculate · Network length
text:
The specific network length times the project area in hectares.
You entered the network length, so it replaces the estimate.

title: How we calculate · Heat density
text: The total heating demand divided by the network length. It is classified in MWh per metre (Table 9).

title: How we calculate · Heating supply
text: For each selected source, the default capacity of its potential plus the share the heat pump adds (COP), summed over all sources. Solar thermal works without a heat pump.

title: How we calculate · Cooling supply
text: For each selected source, the default cooling capacity of its potential adjusted by the COP, summed over all sources. Waste heat and solar thermal supply no cooling.

title: How we calculate · Heating supply coverage
text: The heating supply divided by the heating demand: the share of the annual heating demand the selected sources can cover.

title: How we calculate · Cooling supply coverage
text: The cooling supply divided by the cooling demand: the share of the annual cooling demand the selected sources can cover.

title: How we calculate · Cooling-to-heating ratio
text: The smaller of the heating and cooling demand divided by the larger one. The closer it is to one, the more balanced the demands.

title: How we calculate · Annual heating revenue
text: The heating base price for every m² of floor area per year, plus the heating energy price for every kWh of heating demand.

title: How we calculate · Annual cooling revenue
text: The cooling base price for every m² of floor area per year, plus the cooling energy price for every kWh of cooling demand.

title: How we calculate · Connection fee
text: The one-time connection fee of every building, spread over the depreciation period with the annuity factor.

title: How we calculate · Overall revenues
text: Heating revenue, cooling revenue and the annualized connection fees.

title: How we calculate · Network investment
text: The network construction costs per metre times the network length.

title: How we calculate · Total installation investment
text: For each selected source, its installation costs per kWh/a times its heating supply, summed over all sources. Ambient air adds no installation costs, as the heat pumps are counted separately.

title: How we calculate · Heat pump
text: The investment in one heat pump times the number of buildings.

title: How we calculate · Overall investment
text: Heat pumps, network and the installations of all sources. The installations are counted once.

title: How we calculate · Annuity factor
text: Turns an investment into equal yearly payments over the depreciation period at the interest rate.

title: How we calculate · Annualized costs
text: The overall investment times the annuity factor: its cost per year.

title: How we calculate · Electricity costs
text: The electricity the heat pumps need (supply divided by COP) times the electricity price. With PV, the costs are lowered by the PV cost reduction.

title: How we calculate · Operation and maintenance
text: A fixed share of the overall investment every year.

title: How we calculate · Annual costs
text: Annualized investment, electricity costs, and operation and maintenance costs.

title: How we calculate · Economic ratio
text: The overall revenues divided by the annual costs. The economic assessment rates this ratio as favorable, unclear or clearly unfavorable.

title: How we calculate · Overall result
text: The overall result combines the supply coverage, the building and heat density and the economic assessment (Table 11). Industry in the project area or a source with unknown potential always leads to “Further analysis required”.

title: Quick Check · Overall result
text:
Promising: Favorable conditions identified
Further analysis required: Mixed conditions, uncertainties or missing information
Not promising: Unfavorable conditions identified

title: Quick Check · Supply coverage
text:
Feasible: Sufficient annual energy potential to cover the total demand with additional potential available.
Conditionally feasible: A small share of supplementary supply is required.
Limited feasibility: A significant share of supplementary supply is required.
Not feasible as the sole supply concept: Too much demand remains uncovered.

title: Quick Check · Building density
text:
High density: Densely built areas can benefit from shorter network lengths, although low energy demand may still weaken economic performance.
Medium density: The structure may be suitable for a network.
Low density: Buildings are more distributed, potentially increasing network length. High energy demand or suitable local energy sources may still make a project promising.

title: Quick Check · Heat density
text:
High density: A relatively short network serves a high heating demand, potentially improving economic performance.
Medium density: The network may be viable.
Low density: A relatively long network serves a low heating demand. Substantial cooling demand or low network costs may improve the outlook.

title: Quick Check · Cooling-to-heating ratio
text:
Balanced: Heating and cooling demand are similar, potentially supporting thermal exchange.
Partially balanced: One demand is higher than the other, but thermal exchange may still be possible.
Unbalanced: One demand clearly dominates, potentially increasing the need for external energy sources or thermal storage.

title: Quick Check · Economic assessment
text:
Favorable: The revenues cover the annual costs.
Unclear: The revenues cover a large part, but not all, of the annual costs.
Clearly unfavorable: The revenues fall far short of the annual costs.

title: Quick Check · Screening, not a full feasibility study
text: This is an initial indication based on simplified default values. Actual values depend on project-specific conditions and should be refined through further analysis.

title: Quick Check · Project area
text:
Total number of buildings: All buildings in the project area, including industrial buildings.
Total project area: Enter the area in m². The value in hectares is shown next to it.

title: Quick Check · Buildings
text: Share of buildings: Enter the share of each building type and construction period in %. All shares must add up to 100 %.

title: Quick Check · Energy sources
text: Energy sources: Select the energy sources available or potentially available in the project area and rate their potential.

title: Quick Check · Options
text:
Photovoltaic (PV) available: PV lowers the electricity costs of the heat pumps by the PV cost reduction of Table 6.
Known heating and cooling demand: Optional. If you know the buildings' energy demand, enter it here instead of the default estimate.
Total heating demand: Optional. Replaces the estimated total heating demand.
Total cooling demand: Optional. Replaces the estimated total cooling demand.
Network length: Optional. Leave empty to estimate the length from the building density and the project area.

title: Quick Check · Assumptions
text:
Heating capacity per source (Table 4): Annual capacity per potential level in kWh/a, and the heat pump COP. Leave a cell empty to keep the default.
Cooling capacity per source (Table 5): Annual capacity per potential level in kWh/a, and the COP. Leave a cell empty to keep the default.
Economic parameters (Table 6): Leave a value empty to keep the default.

title: Business Plan · Opportunity
text:
Site or district: Describe the site or district the business model is for.
Location: Municipality, region or country.
Type of site: For example a rural village, the urban outskirts or an existing neighbourhood.
Property and usage types: Who owns the buildings and how they are used, for example private ownership, rental housing or tourism.
Units or buildings: As far as known, for example "20-70 units, phased development".
Current energy supply: One entry per energy carrier, for example natural gas or biomass.
Stakeholders: One entry per stakeholder, for example private households or a hotel.
Other partners: One entry per partner, for example the municipality.
Use case: Start from a predefined scenario or describe your own use case.
The opportunity: What the network is for, and for whom.
Customer segments: Who would connect to the network?
Heating and cooling needs: What heating and cooling do the buildings need?
Relevant heat sources: Which local sources could supply the network, and what is known about them?
Key pain point: What problem does the site have today?
Available alternatives: What else could the buildings do, for example individual heat pumps?

title: Business Plan · Opportunity
text: Why a shared low-temperature network: Why does a shared network offer value compared with the alternatives?

title: Business Plan · Business logic
text:
Business Model Canvas: Pay particular attention to the value proposition, customer relationships, key partners, operator responsibilities, cost structure and revenue streams.
Operator responsibilities: Who owns and operates the source, the network and the heat pumps, and who is responsible for what?
Allocation of investment, risk and benefit: Make explicit who invests, who carries which risk and who benefits.

title: Business Plan · Reality check
text:
Rough assumptions: Use rough but transparent assumptions rather than detailed engineering calculations.
Critical assumptions: The top critical assumptions, and how each could be validated.
Risks: The top risks, including one potential deal-breaker, and how each could be validated.

title: Business Plan · Implementation
text:
Refinements: Refine the business model based on the Reality Check, expert feedback and the challenges found.
Scalability and replication: Could the model work under different geographical, economic and organisational conditions?
Next steps: The next practical steps towards implementation.
